title: Many Cultures, Traditions and Beliefs
keyIdea: A culture is the way of life a group of people shares: food, language, clothes, festivals, and the beliefs and values underneath them. The world holds thousands of cultures. Different cultures often celebrate for the same big reasons, such as light, a new year or the harvest. What feels normal depends on where you grew up, so a new habit is not weird or wrong. Asking respectful questions helps you learn, and ideas shared between cultures make every community richer.

kid: A culture is the way of life a group shares. Some of it you can see: food, clothes, music and the words people speak. Most of it is hidden, like the big part of an iceberg under the sea. That hidden part is what people believe and value, such as how to treat elders or what makes a good life.

Festivals can look very different and still share a reason. Diwali and Hanukkah are both festivals of lights. Lunar New Year and Nowruz both mark a new year. Chuseok, Pongal and Sukkot all give thanks for the harvest. Different ways, same big ideas.

What feels normal depends on where you grew up. Aiko takes her shoes off at home, and shoes inside feel odd to her. Your habits may seem just as new to her. Weird often just means new to me. So ask: What does this mean to your family? Can you show me how?
Lots of what you use came from other cultures. Paper and tea came from China. The digits 0 to 9 began in India. Potatoes came from the Andes in South America. When people share ideas, everyone gains.
adult: This topic sits in the social awareness strand of PSHE. The IB PYP PSPE framework asks children to show interest in and respect for other cultures and beliefs. In England, the PSHE Association programme asks pupils aged 9 to 11 to value diversity. They should respect people whose beliefs, customs and backgrounds differ from their own.

Key terms: culture, tradition, custom, belief, value, festival, diversity, perspective, respect and stereotype. A useful tool is the culture iceberg, from the writer Edward T. Hall. Surface culture is what you can see, such as food, dress and festivals. Deep culture lies below: values, beliefs and ideas about family, respect and time. Most clashes start below the waterline.

Common mistakes: thinking culture is just food, flags and festivals. Calling a custom weird because it is new to you; the term for this is ethnocentrism. Asking questions that are really put-downs. Turning interest into a stereotype, such as 'everyone from Japan eats sushi'. Be careful with the reverse slip too: do not treat one child as the voice of a whole culture. Ask what their own family does.

In the lab the learner sorts a culture iceberg. They match festivals from five traditions to the reason they share. They hear the other child's side when a habit looks odd, and sort kind questions from put-downs and stereotypes. Last, they trace paper, the digits 0 to 9, maize, potatoes and coffee back to where they began.

familyTip: At dinner, each person names one thing in the house that started in another culture (tea, pasta, pyjamas, the digits on the clock). Then ask a grandparent or friend: what did your family celebrate when you were young, and why?

visual.caption: Surface or deep culture? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort a culture iceberg, match festivals to their reason, hear the other side, sort kind questions, and trace things to where they began.

practice.prompt: Many cultures: which of these is deep culture, hidden below the waterline of the iceberg?
choices: What a family believes makes a good life
The food served at a festival
The clothes worn at a wedding
practice.hint: You can see food and clothes. Which one can you not see?
practice.explain: Beliefs and values are deep culture. You cannot see them, but they shape the food, clothes and festivals you can see.

practice.prompt: Hanukkah lasts 8 nights. One candle is lit on the first night, and one more is added each night. How many candles are lit on night {n}?
practice.hint: Night 1 has 1 candle, night 2 has 2 candles. Spot the pattern.
practice.explain: One more candle is added each night, so night {n} has {n} candles, plus the helper candle called the shamash.

practice.prompt: Ben says, 'You eat with your hand? That's weird.' What could he say instead?
choices: Is that how your family eats? Can you show me?
practice.hint: Which one asks to learn, instead of judging?
practice.explain: A curious question shows respect and helps Ben learn. The other two say his own way is the only normal one.

practice.prompt: In a class of {n} children, {k} children celebrate Diwali, and the rest do not. How many children could learn about Diwali from a classmate?
practice.hint: The children who do not celebrate it can learn about it from those who do.
practice.explain: {n} take away {k} is {=n-k} children who could learn something new from a classmate's festival.

pool.prompt: Diwali and Hanukkah come from different faiths. What do they share?
pool.hint: Think about the lamps and the candles.
pool.explain: Diwali has diyas and Hanukkah has a candle for each night. Different stories and faiths share the big idea of light.

pool.prompt: Someone says, 'Everyone from China eats rice every day.' What is this?
pool.hint: Does it treat each person as their own, or the whole group as the same?
pool.explain: It says a whole group is the same. People in any country are all different, so this is a stereotype.

pool.prompt: Where were the digits 0 to 9 that we use for maths first developed?
pool.hint: Roman numerals use letters such as X and V, not 0 to 9.
pool.explain: Our digits, with zero, began in India and reached Europe through Arabic scholars. That is why they are called Hindu-Arabic numerals.

pool.prompt: A school fair has {n} stalls, and each one shares food from a different culture. You try a dish from {k} of them. How many cultures' dishes have you not tried yet?
pool.hint: Take the stalls you visited away from all the stalls.
pool.explain: {n} take away {k} is {=n-k} dishes still to try. Each one is a new taste from another culture.

pool.prompt: Aiko takes her shoes off at home. To her, shoes indoors feel odd. What does this show?
choices: Normal depends on where you grew up
Shoes indoors is the only right way
pool.hint: Is there one normal way for everyone in the world?
pool.explain: Each family's habits feel normal to them. Neither way is wrong; they are different normals.

pool.prompt: Why can lots of cultures in one place make a community stronger?
choices: People share more ideas, words and ways to solve problems
Everyone must give up their own ways
pool.hint: Think of tea, paper and potatoes. Where did they come from?
pool.explain: When people share ideas, everyone gains new foods, words and ways of seeing a problem. Nobody has to give anything up.

pool.prompt: Pongal is a harvest festival that lasts 4 days. Sukkot lasts 7 days. Your friend has been celebrating Sukkot for {n} days. How many days are left?
pool.hint: Sukkot lasts 7 days. Take away the days that have passed.
pool.explain: 7 take away {n} is {=7-n} days of Sukkot left to share meals in the hut.

pool.prompt: Which question is the most respectful way to learn about a classmate's tradition?
choices: What does this tradition mean to your family?
Why do you do that strange thing?
Does everyone in your country do that?
pool.hint: Which one asks about their family, without judging?
pool.explain: It asks about their own family and shows real interest. The others judge the custom or treat a whole country as the same.
